crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting proposals from past work covers the practice of reusing a researcher's own prior proposals, papers, progress reports and reviewer comments as source material for a new funding application. It sits inside grant proposals and funding, where the writing burden is high and the underlying science is often already documented elsewhere. The scope includes assembling a fundable narrative from existing text, not generating new findings, and it spans the whole document from aims and background to budget justification and biosketch.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a document store of the researcher's own past submissions, award reports and publications, plus the funder's current call text and formatting rules. General purpose language models are commonly used to summarise, restructure and rephrase that material, and reference managers or a literature library supply the citations. Where a site library is used, it links to the original paper rather than to a search tool, so the writer can check each source directly.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual method is to gather the relevant past documents, extract the sections that still hold true, and map them onto the new call's headings and page limits. A model is then asked to condense, reorder or rewrite passages, and the researcher edits the output against the funder's review criteria. Claims and citations are checked back to the source paper, and the final text is read as a single argument rather than a set of pasted fragments.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on self plagiarism, duplicate submission rules and confidentiality of unpublished or reviewer material. Funders generally require that a proposal is original to that call, so reused text must be disclosed or rewritten, and prior review comments are not the writer's to circulate freely. Provenance matters because every factual claim and citation should trace to a named paper or dataset, and any model assistance should follow the funder's and the institution's disclosure rules. This is a description of common practice, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter integration between a researcher's publication record and the proposal drafting process, with retrieval over a personal corpus rather than generic generation. Funders are adding disclosure requirements for AI assistance, and institutions are building internal guidance to match. The likely result is that drafting becomes faster at the assembly stage while the originality and provenance checks become more explicit.
